title: HiVid: LLM-Guided Video Saliency For Content-Aware VOD And Live Streaming
one_liner: HiVid estimates how important each video chunk is for perceived viewing quality, using large language models for offline labeling and a separate predictor to forecast future chunk importance during live streaming.
lead: Content-aware streaming needs a weight for each video chunk: which moments deserve more bits because viewers care more about them, and which moments can be compressed harder with limited visible damage. Human labeling of those weights is expensive, but purely visual saliency systems often miss semantics such as speech turns, object interactions, or event importance. HiVid uses a large language model as a scalable labeling agent. For video on demand, it scores local windows and then re-ranks them globally. For live streaming, where the future frames are unknown, it trains a predictor that estimates upcoming importance from past content and past weights.

problem.h2: Why chunk importance is hard to estimate
paras: Adaptive streaming already changes bitrate across time, but content-aware streaming needs a more informative signal than motion magnitude or scene cuts because those low-level cues miss semantic importance. It needs chunk importance: a score that says which parts of the video matter more to perceived quality. A close-up during a key action, a slide with dense text, and a quiet background pan should not receive the same treatment.

Direct human scoring does not scale because long videos contain thousands of chunks, and consistency across raters is limited. Pure vision saliency models also struggle because importance is semantic: the decisive moment may be defined by dialogue, intent, or the continuation of an earlier event rather than by raw pixel change.

The paper addresses this with a three-part system. A perception stage interprets local windows with an LLM, a ranking stage fixes local inconsistency across the whole video, and a prediction stage estimates future chunk importance when streaming must act before the future video arrives.

callout.html: Use an LLM to score local windows as a human proxy, reconcile those local scores into a global ordering for stored video, and train an online predictor that forecasts future chunk importance for live streaming.

panels.title: 1. Video becomes chunks
panels.caption: Each segment needs its own importance weight for bitrate allocation.

panels.title: 2. Local windows are scored
panels.caption: An LLM judges which chunks in each short window matter most.

panels.title: 3. Window scores can conflict
panels.caption: A chunk can be rated high inside one window and only medium inside another nearby window.

panels.title: 4. Global re-ranking resolves conflicts
panels.caption: For stored video, pairwise comparisons are merged into a consistent ranking over the whole timeline.

panels.title: 5. Live mode predicts ahead
panels.caption: A forecasting model estimates near-future weights so the encoder can act before the next chunks arrive.

steps.text: Split the video into short windows and ask an LLM to rate chunk importance inside each window while accumulating context from previous windows.
For stored video, compare chunks across windows and merge those comparisons into one global ranking of chunk importance.
Use the LLM-produced weights as supervision for a separate time-series predictor that consumes recent content features and recent weights.
During live streaming, the predictor estimates the importance of upcoming chunks without seeing future frames.
The streaming system spends more bits on higher-weight chunks and compresses lower-weight chunks more aggressively.

paras: The paper changes the target signal used by the streaming controller. Instead of relying on raw heuristics such as motion or edge strength, it builds chunk weights from semantic judgments produced by an LLM and then predicts those weights online. This matters because the encoder needs a signal that reflects viewer importance, not only pixel activity.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: chunk saliency weight
hidden.name: How much visible quality a chunk deserves relative to others
paras: The main quantity is the chunk saliency weight: a scalar (one number) assigned to each chunk that summarizes how much quality budget it should receive. A high weight means visible degradation in that chunk is likely to matter more to viewers. A low weight means the same bitrate cut is less noticeable or less important to the experience.

Estimating this quantity is hard because importance depends on context. A frame with little motion may still be decisive if it contains a key subtitle or a diagnostic chart. HiVid first estimates weights with an LLM over local windows, then adjusts them so the whole video has a consistent ordering, and finally learns to predict them from recent history for live use.

heat.caption: Darker means the chunk should receive more bitrate because visible quality matters more there.

reads.html: The system is trying to answer one question for every chunk: if bitrate is limited, where does picture quality matter most?
HiVid uses LLM-derived chunk weights as high-fidelity supervision for both global VOD ranking and online live-stream prediction.

mechanism.h2: Why the three modules fit together
paras: The perception module solves local semantic understanding. An LLM can inspect a short window and judge whether a slide, gesture, or event is likely to matter to a viewer. That produces detailed local scores, but those scores are only relative to the current window and can drift across time.

The ranking module solves that drift by comparing chunks across windows and merging the comparisons into one timeline-wide ordering. The prediction module solves the live setting, where future frames are unavailable. It learns from past LLM labels so it can estimate upcoming weights from recent multimodal history. This works by separating expensive semantic labeling from cheap real-time forecasting.

math.words: Learn a predictor whose future chunk weights match the LLM-generated reference weights while staying usable with only past information.
math.equation: hat(w)_(t+h) = P(x_1:t, w_1:t, h), minimize sum_h |hat(w)_(t+h) - w_(t+h)^LLM|
symbols: predicted weight for a future chunk h steps ahead
content features observed up to time t
past chunk weights up to time t
reference weight assigned by the LLM-based labeling pipeline

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the last few chunks were a calm introduction, then a slide appears with dense text, and a key spoken point is about to continue.
The predictor receives the recent content features and recent weights, then estimates the next three chunk weights as 0.4, 0.8, and 0.75.
Later, the offline LLM labeling pipeline assigns reference weights 0.35, 0.9, and 0.7 to those chunks.
The prediction error is small on the first and third chunks and larger on the second, so training pushes the model to react more strongly when text-heavy or event-heavy segments begin.

math.note: The live predictor never sees future frames. It succeeds only when recent context carries enough information to anticipate what viewers will care about next.

charts.title: Motion-based or saliency-only baseline
charts.note: Simple baselines can run online, but they miss many chunks whose importance depends on meaning rather than motion.

charts.title: HiVid
charts.note: Offline LLM labeling provides richer targets, and the learned predictor makes those targets usable in the live setting.

items.html: A chunk may matter because of an event many seconds earlier. If the accumulated context is weak, the LLM can assign a low score to a chunk that is actually important in the full narrative.

items.b: Global re-ranking can inherit noisy comparisons.
items.html: The merge-sort stage only reconciles the local judgments it receives. If many pairwise comparisons are wrong, the final ranking is coherent but still misplaced.

items.b: Live prediction breaks under abrupt shifts.
items.html: A sudden event that has no precursor in recent content is hard to forecast because the predictor only sees the past and current stream.

Use the LLM pipeline to produce stable supervision on stored video, train the live predictor on varied temporal patterns, and let the bitrate controller combine predicted weights with standard network constraints.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a small set of lecture videos, sports clips, and livestream replays. Produce chunk weights with human raters, with a motion-based baseline, and with HiVid. Then use those weights inside the same bitrate allocator and compare the resulting quality allocation. For live mode, hold out the future frames and test whether the predictor still raises weights before important moments.
demo.metric_eq: Correlation with human chunk weights, weighted video quality, and live prediction error over future horizons
demo.closing: The demo should show that the main gain comes from better importance targets: the encoder spends bits on chunks that viewers actually care about, because the weights track semantic importance instead of only motion, and the live predictor preserves part of that benefit even without future access.
